🧠 PySpark Window Functions — The Secret Weapon Most Data Engineers Overlook

If you’re still relying solely on groupBy() in your PySpark pipelines, it’s time to level up.

While groupBy() is great for collapsing data and summarizing across groups, it destroys the row-level context. That’s where Window Functions come in — they give you the power to perform complex analytics without collapsing the data.

⸻

⚙️ What Can You Do With Window Functions?

With just a few lines of code, you can:
✅ Get the latest record per user
✅ Rank items within each category
✅ Compare a row to its previous or next one
✅ Compute running totals, moving averages, and more

All while preserving every row in your dataset.

🎯 Why This Matters

As Data Engineers, we often work with time-based event logs, user histories, or ranking scenarios.

Window functions let us solve these problems cleanly, keeping the dataset intact, scalable, and readable.

⸻

If you’re not using them yet, start today.
Your future self (and your pipelines) will thank you.

The post does not provide code or implementation details.

interview_questions.question: How do PySpark window functions differ from groupBy() when processing data?
interview_questions.answer:
groupBy() collapses records into group-level summaries and therefore removes row-level context.
Window functions perform analytical calculations while preserving every row in the dataset.

interview_questions.question: What analytical tasks can PySpark window functions perform without collapsing the data?
interview_questions.answer:
They can identify the latest record per user and rank items within categories.
They can compare a row with its previous or next row.
They can compute running totals and moving averages while retaining every row.

interview_questions.question: A PySpark pipeline must analyze user histories while retaining individual records. Why would window functions be more suitable than relying only on groupBy()?
interview_questions.answer:
Window functions preserve the records and row-level context needed for user-history analysis.
Using only groupBy() would collapse the data into summaries and remove individual row context.
Window functions can support tasks such as finding the latest record for each user without collapsing the dataset.
